extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, graduate students, and researchers interested in research practice and career advice
extracted.subtask_short: acknowledge tool limits in math papers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for mathematicians on recognizing, testing, and communicating the limits of methods and tools in research and publications, so that results are properly qualified and future work is guided. Emphasizes deep understanding, counterexamples, and transparent exposition of what a technique cannot prove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish knowledge from understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: "An education isn't how much you have committed to memory, or even how much you know. It's being able to differentiate between what you do know and what you don't." (Anatole France, cited by Tao.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't confuse memorized facts or routine manipulations with genuine understanding. A mathematician should be able to say precisely what aspects of a problem they truly understand versus what they merely know how to compute or apply; this clarity prevents overclaiming and directs further learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when tools fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand where your methods don't work to prevent wasted effort on doomed strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the domains, hypotheses, or structural features where a tool or method is inapplicable or breaks down. Use this knowledge to avoid pursuing approaches that are unlikely to succeed and to choose alternate strategies more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a library of counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain model situations and obstructions that reveal which problems your tools can and cannot address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively collect and study counterexamples, borderline cases, and obstructions as a diagnostic resource. These examples help you recognize failure modes of techniques quickly and sharpen intuition about the true reach of a method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the "magic wand" trap
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not view a tool as mysteriously solving problems without deeper comprehension; this indicates insufficient foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you treat a method as a black-box that 'magically' resolves difficulties, pause and seek a deeper conceptual basis. Reliance on unexplained or poorly understood steps can lead to errors and limit the ability to adapt techniques to new problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test understanding through reconstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving significant results, try to rewrite arguments without your preferred tool; if impossible, you may be misapplying the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reconstruction exercises (re-deriving proofs or arguments using different approaches) as a test of genuine understanding. Failure to reconstruct suggests dependence on accidental features of a tool rather than structural insight, signaling the need for deeper analysis or alternate methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss limitations in publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparently addressing known constraints builds credibility and guides future research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing papers or reports, explicitly state what the argument or method cannot show, the hypotheses on which the conclusions depend, and plausible routes that would be needed to overcome these limitations. Such candor helps readers assess the result's scope and aids subsequent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematics acknowledges tool limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' paper acknowledges its tools' limits — what its argument cannot show — rather than presenting the technique as omnipotent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work by whether it clearly demarcates the reach of its techniques and avoids implying broader applicability than justified. Papers that carefully state limitations and contexts for validity are judged more trustworthy and useful to the community.
